title: Catering
primary_metric: net profit (revenue - ingredient cost - event fee - delivery fee)

options.B: Take the Adobitron corporate party order

new_coverage_note: CORRECTED 2026-08-04: the originally-claimed new_coverage (measurement-how-to-find-a-missing-amount-in-a-proportion) turned out already covered -- 'Wildfire', a pre-existing legacy-matrix case, already carried this skill from before this pipeline's own work began, so it was never actually n=0. Every other originally-claimed skill was also already heavily covered elsewhere (n=21-29). Real new coverage was added instead: D5 asks the Hero to solve for the minimum servings the chosen event needs for its net profit to cover Victorino's real $950 monthly loan payment (now stated in Background), using the event's own real per-serving margin and fees from D3 -- isolating servings on one side of `margin*s - fees = 950` is a genuine forcing task for 'variable on one side' (n=0 pre-conversion). The real answer for the wedding (123 servings) exceeds its actual booked order (118 servings) -- a genuine finding: as booked, the wedding's real profit ($897.42) falls $52.58 short of covering the loan payment, which is new information for D6's recommendation. D5 is ordered before D6 (recommendation) deliberately, after a QA simulation on a sibling case (Archery Camp) found the opposite order let Heroes recommend before the fact that should inform the recommendation existed.
legacy_conversion_note: Original 2021 case's menu prices, ingredient costs, and fee structure (event fee, delivery fee, 7% excess-food buffer) are as authored in the original legacy case study material -- invented scenario data for a fictional small catering business, not sourced from or representing any real external company. (The business name 'Maggiano's Cucina' coincidentally resembles the real national chain Maggiano's Little Italy; this case's founder Victorino, his backstory, prices, and two-person kitchen are entirely fictional and have no connection to that real company -- flagged here so a facilitator who recognizes the name isn't confused about what is and isn't real in this case.) Appendix A (the actual two client orders: guest counts, chosen menu items) was blank in the source .docx (a placeholder line, never filled in) -- this conversion designs its own concrete, realistic order specifications (guest counts, menu selections, event length) as the case's own given scenario data, the same authorial latitude a human case-write author has when specifying 'the order' a case is built around. Delivery mileage between the stated addresses (Appendix E) is disclosed as a reasonable estimate (Appendix C, Assumption 2), not a routed/sourced figure. The 'total prep time' deliverable in the original Challenge 3 was dropped: no prep-time-per-dish data exists anywhere in the source material, and inventing one would violate the never-fabricate-a-number rule.

modeling_assumptions.text: The 7% excess-food buffer (Appendix C) rounds up to the next whole serving -- Maggiano's Cucina cannot prepare a fractional serving.

Round-trip delivery distance is estimated at 8 miles to the Millennial Falls Event Center and 18 miles to Adobitron HQ (Appendix C, Assumption 2) -- reasonable estimates for the area, not routed or sourced.

deliverables.text: Total servings to prepare, set up and solved as a proportion from the 7% buffer rule.
Total revenue and total ingredient cost for the chosen event's menu.
Total fees (event fee and delivery fee) for the chosen event.
Net profit: revenue minus ingredient cost minus total fees.
Solve for the minimum number of servings the chosen event's order would need for its net profit alone to cover Victorino's $950 monthly loan payment.
A recommendation comparing both events' net profit, computed the same way, informed by D5's finding.

balance.argument_a: The Beal wedding nets $897.42 after every fee -- $2,245.89 in gross profit against $575 in event fees and just $13.20 in delivery (the venue is in the same city as the kitchen). Its 118-serving order (110 guests, rounded up from 110 x 1.07 = 117.7) has real, consistent per-serving margins across all three menu items.
balance.argument_b: The Adobitron party nets $760.62 -- lower, but on a smaller 107-serving order at 100 guests, meaning a comparable margin per guest actually served, with a genuinely more consistent, recurring client type (Background: Maggiano's is already seeing more corporate repeat business than seasonal weddings). A slightly lower one-time profit on an event type that tends to reorder is a real, defensible trade against a slightly higher profit on a type that historically doesn't.
balance.margin_basis: Net profit (revenue - ingredient cost - event fee - delivery fee) for each event as specified in Appendix A, computed from Appendix B/C/D's real given pricing and fee structure. See derived{} for the full worked figures.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendix A-D's given data; case-readiness should re-derive independently, not just trust this block.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: corporate_miles is Appendix C Assumption 2's own disclosed round-trip mileage estimate to Adobitron HQ -- the case text already states it is 'a reasonable estimate for the area, not a routed, sourced figure.' Adobitron is a fictional company invented for this case (no real Lehi, UT address exists to route against), so the 18-mile figure cannot be tightened by further research the way a real business's address could be -- there is no more-precise real value to look up. At +50% flex (18mi -> 27mi) the corporate party's delivery fee rises enough to push the case's own margin from 17.99% to 20.3%, breaking SPEC §2's 20% cap; buffer_pct and wedding_miles both stay stable across the full ±50% range. This is a real, reproducible instability in one of the case's two named modeling_assumptions (MA2), disclosed here rather than eliminated by inventing a false-precision routed distance for a location that does not exist.

cohort_bands.note: Anchors 2-3 run as written; the room debates one-time profit vs. recurring-client type before the ceiling math settles part of it.
Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; D1/D2 are worked for one event together instead of both events independently first.
No vote to take -- Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a cold-call; guide plays devil's advocate directly.
